prompt: Which of these can change data capture see that a watermark on `updated_at` cannot? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: A deleted row
choices.why: Yes. The delete is written to the log like any change.

choices.text: An order's state before a later update the same day
choices.why: Yes. Each change arrives, not just the latest state.

choices.text: An update that forgot to set `updated_at`
choices.why: Yes. The log records the write whatever columns it touched.

choices.text: A row that was never committed
choices.why: A rolled-back transaction never reaches the stream.

prompt: Why does PostgreSQL keep a write-ahead log in the first place?
hint: It was not built for pipelines.

choices.text: To feed change data capture tools
choices.why: That is a later use of something built for another reason.

choices.text: To survive a crash
choices.why: Right. It replays the log after a crash, and replicas follow it too.

choices.text: To keep an audit trail of who changed what
choices.why: The WAL records changes, not who made them.

choices.text: To make queries faster
choices.why: Queries read tables; the WAL makes writes durable.

prompt: A till's transaction is written at 23:40 and commits at 00:05. Where does it appear in the slot's stream?
hint: The stream is in one particular order.

choices.text: At 23:40, among the changes written then
choices.why: Nothing appears before it commits.

choices.text: Nowhere, because it took too long
choices.why: Duration does not matter; committing does.

choices.text: At 00:05, its commit
choices.why: Right. The stream is in commit order, so the slow till's problem disappears.

choices.text: Twice, once when written and once when committed
choices.why: Each committed transaction arrives once, whole.

prompt: The slot held 1,088 lines for 1 March, from 211 transactions. Each transaction adds a BEGIN and a COMMIT line. How many lines were row changes?
A byte position in PostgreSQL's write-ahead log is called a log sequence number, abbreviated ___.
What is the difference between `pg_logical_slot_peek_changes` and `pg_logical_slot_get_changes`?
hint: One of them moves the slot.

choices.text: `peek` shows only inserts
choices.why: It shows every change, like `get`.

choices.text: `get` consumes them
choices.why: Right. `peek` reads without consuming, so it can be repeated.

choices.text: `get` needs the replication protocol
choices.why: Both are ordinary SQL functions.

choices.text: `peek` reads the WAL from disk, `get` from memory
choices.why: Both decode the same WAL; one of them advances the slot.

prompt: Why did Ana create the slot before copying the customers whole, and not after?
hint: What could happen between the copy and the slot?

choices.text: A slot refuses to start on a table that has been copied
choices.why: A slot knows nothing about copies.

choices.text: Copying first is slower
choices.why: The order changes correctness, not speed.

choices.text: The copy needs the slot's LSN as a file name
choices.why: The copy is an ordinary `\copy`.

choices.text: So nothing committed in between falls through the gap
choices.why: Right. Changes during the copy are in the slot, and applying them twice is harmless.

prompt: `apply_cdc.py` writes to the warehouse, and the warehouse commits; then the shop's connection fails before its commit. What happens next time?
hint: The slot moves only when the shop's transaction commits.

choices.text: The changes are lost
choices.why: The slot did not move, so they are still there.

choices.text: They come again, harmlessly
choices.why: Right. Upserts and deletes by key leave the same rows.

choices.text: The warehouse rolls back to match
choices.why: It committed; nothing rolls it back.

choices.text: PostgreSQL refuses to decode the slot until it is reset
choices.why: The slot is fine; it just has not moved.

prompt: `apply_cdc.py` reads 666 changes to apply 23 to customers. What would a production setup use to avoid reading the rest?
hint: A list of tables the database honours.

choices.text: A publication, with the `pgoutput` plugin
choices.why: Right. The reader receives only the tables it asked for.

choices.text: A `WHERE` clause on `get_changes`
choices.why: That filters after decoding and still consumes everything.

choices.text: One slot per table, all with `test_decoding`
choices.why: Every slot would decode every table's changes.

choices.text: A trigger that copies customer changes to another table
choices.why: That is a different design; the slot still sees every table.

prompt: What does `ALTER TABLE customers REPLICA IDENTITY FULL` add to each update in the stream?

choices.text: The name of the user who made the change
choices.why: Replica identity is about the old row, not the user.

choices.text: A checksum of the new row
choices.why: No checksum is added.

choices.text: The whole old row
choices.why: Right. A history can now say where the customer lived before.

choices.text: The primary key only
choices.why: That is the default, before `FULL`.

prompt: Why does the lesson call `REPLICA IDENTITY FULL` a decision for the source's owner rather than for the pipeline?

choices.text: Only superusers can run `ALTER TABLE`
choices.why: The table's owner can; the point is the cost.

choices.text: The source pays for the extra WAL
choices.why: Right. The system taking sales carries the extra writing.

choices.text: It changes the table's primary key
choices.why: The key is unchanged.

choices.text: It stops the tills while it runs
choices.why: It is a quick catalogue change.

prompt: The forgotten slot held back 6,085 kB after fourteen days. About how many kB a day is that? Give a whole number.
A team switches off its CDC pipeline for a migration and forgets its slot. A month later the source database stops accepting writes. Why?

choices.text: The slot locked the tables it was reading
choices.why: Slots take no table locks.

choices.text: The kept WAL filled the disk the database lives on
choices.why: Right. A month of WAL, held for a reader that never came back.

choices.text: PostgreSQL limits a database to one slot
choices.why: The lab had two at once.

choices.text: The `wal_level` setting reverted
choices.why: Nothing reverts it.

prompt: Match each defence against a forgotten slot to what it does.
hint: One limits, one warns, one removes.

pairs.right: Invalidates the slot before the disk fills
Shows how much WAL each slot holds

prompt: With `max_slot_wal_keep_size` set, a forgotten slot passes the limit. What happens, and why is that the right way round?

choices.text: The database stops writes until the slot is read
choices.why: That is what happens without a limit.

choices.text: The oldest WAL is compressed
choices.why: Nothing is compressed; the slot is invalidated.

choices.text: The slot is invalidated and the source survives
choices.why: Right. Losing the pipeline's place is cheaper than stopping the tills.

choices.text: The slot moves forward on its own and skips the oldest changes
choices.why: It is invalidated, and a reader that relied on it has to start again.

prompt: What does exporting the slot's snapshot give the initial copy?
hint: The copy and the stream start at one moment.

choices.text: A faster copy
choices.why: Speed is not what it buys.

choices.text: The stream's own starting moment
choices.why: Right. Nothing missed, nothing applied twice.

choices.text: A copy that includes rolled-back transactions
choices.why: Snapshots see committed data only.

choices.text: A copy in JSON instead of CSV
choices.why: Format has nothing to do with it.

prompt: When does the lesson recommend the outbox pattern over CDC on the source's tables?
hint: Who has to write the outbox rows?

choices.text: When the source is a database nobody will change
choices.why: Then the outbox cannot be added; CDC on the tables is the tool.

choices.text: When the pipeline has no network access to Kafka
choices.why: The transport is a separate question.

choices.text: When its developers will write the events
choices.why: Right. They write the events, and the internal tables stay free to change.

choices.text: Whenever deletes matter
choices.why: CDC on the tables sees deletes too.

prompt: Order the steps Ana took to keep `cdc.customers` current.
hint: The slot comes before the copy.
items: Read and apply the slot's changes each night

prompt: A colleague proposes replacing `apply_cdc.py`'s upsert with a plain `INSERT`, since every customer change is an insert or an update. What breaks?
hint: An update is for a key that already exists.

choices.text: Nothing: an insert and an update carry the same columns
choices.why: The columns match; the key collides.

choices.text: Deletes stop working
choices.why: Deletes are a separate branch.

choices.text: The slot stops advancing
choices.why: The slot advances on commit, whatever the statements were.

choices.text: Every update fails on the primary key, and so does a repeated change
choices.why: Right. The upsert is what makes both updates and repeats work.
